body.heading: Flips, turns and slides
paragraphs: Symmetry means a shape stays the same after some movement. The most familiar kind is reflection symmetry: fold a butterfly along its body line and the wings match. Most animal bodies, leaves and human faces are approximately mirror-symmetric - approximately, because nature always leaves small imperfections, and spotting them is part of the fun.

Then there is rotational symmetry: a snowflake looks the same after a turn of 60 degrees, a starfish after 72 degrees. And translational symmetry is the pattern of footprints in sand or a brick wall - the same motif slid along, again and again.

body.heading: Why symmetry is everywhere
paragraphs: Symmetry is economical. A body plan mirrored left-to-right needs only half the instructions, and balanced bodies move well through water and air. Flowers use radial symmetry to welcome pollinators from every direction, and crystals grow symmetrically because their atoms stack in repeating arrangements.

Humans are wired to notice symmetry too - we find it in faces, tools, logos and architecture, and artists from every culture have built with it. But artists also know that breaking symmetry, just slightly and in the right place, is what makes a pattern feel alive rather than printed.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Fold a sheet of paper, cut shapes into the fold, and unfold a snowflake or a chain of figures. Then go on a symmetry audit: how many capital letters have a vertical mirror line? (A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y do.) Which have a horizontal one instead, or both?

For a harder hunt, take a photo of a face - with permission - and flip one half in an editor to build two perfectly symmetrical versions. Both will look strangely unlike the real person, which tells you how much character lives in the asymmetries.

takeaway: Symmetry is a pattern that stays the same after a flip, turn or slide - and spotting which kind is a game you can play anywhere.
